description: Somos estudiantes de Ingeniería de Software de la UPChiapas con experiencia en desarrollo web y móvil, backend, bases de datos, nube, ciberseguridad y diseño. Nos interesa crear soluciones tecnológicas para problemas reales y aprender en equipo. Buscamos personas colaborativas con habilidades o interés en ciencia de datos, sistemas geográficos, ciencias de la Tierra, visualización e investigación. Valoramos la comunicación, la iniciativa y la responsabilidad compartida.
summary:
SpectraHive is a citizen science web app that helps people inspect changes in
infrared sky images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Users explore a sky region,
switch between two observation epochs, inspect an absolute difference image,
and report a possible anomaly or mark the region as clean. The interface
distinguishes apparent motion from changes in brightness, and shows a
precomputed “Cosmic DNA” visual spectral signature for comparison. Reports are
sent to a backend for cross-checking; any simulated validation votes in the
demo are clearly labeled. We tested the experience with the five objects named
in the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. By turning complex observations into
focused review tasks, SpectraHive makes public space data easier to explore
and helps demonstrate how people can contribute to astronomical discovery.
details:
SpectraHive turns the inspection of SPHEREx infrared observations into a
focused citizen science task. The user selects one of the five test objects
named in the challenge or opens a shareable sky position using right
ascension, declination, and a field of view of 1° or 2°. An Aladin Lite sky
map provides context. For a selected region, the app displays two observation
epochs, lets the user blink between them, and presents an absolute difference
image, |B−A|. A threshold and candidate information help explain which changes
merit inspection.

The five test objects cover two different behaviors. Barnard’s Star, Epsilon
Indi B, and WISE 0855 are motion examples; RW Aurigae and R Draconis are
brightness variation examples. The interface keeps these interpretations
separate. A user can select a sky position, report motion or brightness
variation, or mark the region as clean. The frontend sends reports to the
FastAPI backend, which handles data processing and persistence. Demo
validation votes are identified as simulated. The “Cosmic DNA” view displays
a precomputed visual spectral signature for comparison; it does not claim
direct chemical identification.

The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Aladin Lite, and
Lucide icons. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, NumPy,
and SciPy to work with SPHEREx images from NASA’s IRSA archive. Supabase
PostgreSQL stores project records. The backend is containerized with Docker.
Our aim is to make public infrared observations approachable while preserving
the distinction between a visual candidate and a validated finding.
dataRefs: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 Spectral Images at IRSA
